The description's root cause is wrong. A symbol lookup miss means mlxc.dll loaded and is a different version than the bindings were generated against. A CUDA variant on a machine without CUDA fails earlier, at LoadLibrary, and that path is already silent. The linked issue was a stale DLL after upgrade; say that.

Moving the message into initLoadError is fine. For the C side, follow x/mlxrunner/xgrammar/dynamic.c: a static const char* load_error that the load macro assigns from the literal, and one accessor that returns it. No buffer, no copy, no record function.

On quantization for direct imports: mlx_lm keeps the granitemoe router at 8 bits; we should do the equivalent. Right now `--quantize` on the original checkpoint quantizes the router at 4 bits and leaves the experts at bf16 (the 3D names don't match isStackedExpertWeight). Adding `.block_sparse_moe.router.layer.weight` to isRoutingGate and the granite expert names to isStackedExpertWeight covers it — just make sure switch_mlp.down_proj and output_linear come out at the same precision.

I reviewed the change and I think this is the right narrow fix for the default `thinking` + `tools` failure mode.

The important part is that this does not change explicit client behavior: if a client asks for `think: true`, Ollama still honors that. It only changes the ambiguous/default case where the model supports thinking, tools are present, and the client did not express a thinking preference.

That is the case causing the practical breakage for OpenAI-compatible agent clients: Ollama silently promotes `req.Think == nil` to thinking enabled, the model may place tool-call intent inside the thinking block, the reasoning gets stripped, and the tool parser never receives usable tool-call tokens. The result is `content: ""` with no `tool_calls`.

This patch makes the safer default choice for tool workflows:

* no tools + no explicit preference: keep thinking on
* tools + no explicit preference: default thinking off
* explicit `think` preference: preserve caller intent
* non-thinking models: unchanged

The implementation is appropriately small: one helper, one call-site update, and a unit test covering the default policy.

I also like that this keeps the deeper explicit-`think: true` + tools behavior scoped separately. That can still be addressed later in parser/template work, but this PR removes the server-side default that currently breaks clients that never opted into thinking.

Given the small surface area, preserved explicit behavior, and the compatibility benefit for tool-calling clients, I support merging this.

I added a conservative escape path for the case where a literal
<tool_call|> appears inside the arguments but no real close tag follows soon
after the completed argument object.

The parser still prefers a real <tool_call|> after the argument object closes.
It only flushes early when the arguments are structurally complete and strictly
parseable, and either no close tag appears within a small lookahead window or a
subsequent <|tool_call> / <|tool_response> boundary appears first.

I intentionally avoided using repair logic for that early-flush decision. If
strict parsing fails, the parser falls through to the existing close-tag or
done-time fallback behavior instead of interpreting malformed arguments
prematurely.

More generally, I’m trying to keep the parser’s responsibility narrow here. It is
hard to recover every malformed generation reliably without risking false
positives, so this PR focuses on the boundary issue we can identify structurally:
a literal <tool_call|> inside arguments should not terminate the tool call.

The resume path re-hashes existing partial data by reading the `.tmp` file through `io.CopyN(h, f, existingSize)` before appending. This is correct for integrity, but for a 64MB minimum threshold this is a full sequential read on every retry before any bytes are downloaded. If a download fails repeatedly (flaky network, server throttling) the re-hash cost compounds. `save` has two `f.Close()` calls — one explicit near the end before the hash check, and one via `defer f.Close()` at the top. After the explicit close, the deferred close will call `Close()` on an already-closed file. On Linux this returns an error that's silently discarded, but it's a latent bug. Remove the explicit `f.Close()` and rely on the defer, or assign `f = nil` after the explicit close and guard the defer.

`TestResumePartialFileExactSize` sets up a `.tmp` file with the full correct content and a server that returns 416 if `start >= blobSize`. The test passes because the server handles that case, but the "completed .tmp" scenario isn't actually being exercised as a resume — it's just a normal full download over an existing file. The behavior here should either be: detect size match, skip the download entirely and just rename, or the test comment needs correcting.

`TestResumeCorruptPartialFile` relies on the retry loop recovering after a hash mismatch. The hash mismatch path calls `os.Remove(tmp)` and returns an error, then `download()` retries. On retry, no `.tmp` exists so it does a fresh full download. This works, but the test doesn't verify that a Range header was *not* sent on the second attempt (after the corrupt partial was removed). It only checks the final file hash. A server that always honors Range headers for any offset would still pass even if the retry incorrectly tried to resume a nonexistent partial.

I get the problem — GPU drivers not ready at service start, Ollama falls back to CPU, users wonder why inference is slow. But graphical.target is the wrong fix for this.
graphical.target means "the display manager and desktop environment are up." That's a much stronger dependency than "GPU drivers are loaded." On a headless server (which is a very common Ollama deployment — no desktop, just SSH), graphical.target may never be reached, meaning the service would never start at all. That's a regression for a significant chunk of users.
The actual problem is that the NVIDIA/AMD kernel modules aren't loaded yet when Ollama starts. Better approaches:

After=systemd-modules-load.service — waits for kernel modules listed in /etc/modules-load.d/ to finish loading. This is closer to what you actually need.
Wants=modprobe@nvidia.service or similar, if the driver is loaded via modprobe.
A ConditionPathExists=/dev/nvidia0 or an ExecStartPre check that waits for the device node, with a retry/restart policy on the service.
systemd-udev-settle.service if the driver is loaded via udev rules.

Any of these would target the actual dependency (GPU driver loaded) without coupling Ollama to a full desktop session. Would suggest exploring one of these before merging.

### Analysis

The fix replaces `strings.Split(s, ",")` with `strings.FieldsFunc(s, func(r rune) bool { return r == ',' })`. The key behavioral difference:

- `strings.FieldsFunc("a,b,,c,", ...)` returns `["a", "b", "c"]` (3 elements, no empty strings)

`FieldsFunc` splits on runs of delimiters and trims leading/trailing delimiters, which is the right semantics for a comma-separated list.

## Overview
This change addresses issue #14766 by fixing false positive matches in the `IsDenied` function. The original implementation used naive substring matching against the full command string, which incorrectly flagged heredoc content and substrings within words (e.g., "su" matching inside "result" or "ensure").

The fix introduces two key improvements:
1. Heredoc bodies are stripped before pattern matching to prevent content inside heredocs from triggering deny patterns
2. Command-like patterns (sudo, su, nc, etc.) are only matched when they appear at actual shell command positions

---

## Analysis

### Key Changes

1. **New Helper: `stripHeredocs`**
   - Uses regex `<<-?\s*['"]?(\w+)['"]?` to match heredoc openers with various quoting styles
   - Properly handles both `<<` and `<<-` (dash-variant for tab-stripping)
   - Locates closing delimiters on their own lines and removes the body content
   - Preserves the heredoc opener line for context

2. **New Helper: `matchesAtCommandPosition`**
   - Checks if a pattern appears at the start of the command or after shell operators: `|`, `&&`, `||`, `;`, `(`, newline, tab
   - Handles whitespace trimming before the match position
   - Iterates through all occurrences of a pattern to find valid command-position matches

3. **New Data: `commandPatterns` Map**
   - Identifies which deny patterns should only match at command positions
   - Includes: sudo, su, doas, nc, netcat, scp, rsync, chown, chgrp, history, mkfifo, shred, mkfs
   - Note: Patterns include trailing spaces where appropriate (e.g., "sudo ") to avoid matching "sudoer"

4. **Updated `IsDenied` Logic**
   - Strips heredocs before checking command patterns
   - Applies position-aware matching only to patterns in `commandPatterns`
   - Falls back to simple substring matching for other deny patterns
   - Checks path patterns against the original command (including heredocs) since paths are specific enough

5. **Test Coverage**
   - Added `TestStripHeredocs` with cases for no heredoc, quoted/unquoted heredocs, and content after heredocs
   - Added test cases for false positive prevention: heredoc bodies, substrings in words, commands after shell operators

---

## Strengths

1. **Targeted Fix**: The solution directly addresses the root causes identified in the issue without over-engineering.

2. **Heredoc Handling**: The regex and parsing logic correctly handles common heredoc variations:
   - Quoted delimiters: `<< 'EOF'`, `<< "EOF"`
   - Unquoted delimiters: `<< EOF`
   - Dash variant for tab-stripping: `<<-EOF`

3. **Position-Aware Matching**: The `matchesAtCommandPosition` function correctly identifies shell command boundaries, preventing false positives from substrings within arguments or data.

4. **Selective Application**: Only command-like patterns use position-aware matching; path patterns and other deny patterns continue to use simple substring matching, which is appropriate for their use cases.

5. **Comprehensive Tests**: The test suite covers:
   - Heredoc stripping edge cases
   - False positive scenarios (substrings in words, heredoc content)
   - True positive scenarios (commands after shell operators)
   - Existing functionality to prevent regressions

6. **Preserves Path Pattern Behavior**: Path patterns like `.env` are checked against the full command including heredocs, which is correct since path matches are specific and should not be suppressed.

---

## Considerations

1. **Heredoc Parsing Edge Cases**:
   - The current implementation assumes the closing delimiter appears on its own line with optional whitespace. This matches bash behavior, but consider documenting this assumption.
   - Nested heredocs are not handled (bash does not support true nesting, but heredoc delimiters can appear in quoted strings within heredoc bodies). This is acceptable since the goal is to strip content, not perfectly parse bash.
   - Heredocs with variable expansion or command substitution in the body are still stripped, which is the intended behavior.

2. **Command Position Detection**:
   - The `commandPrefixes` list covers common shell operators but may not be exhaustive. Consider whether backticks, `$()`, or other command substitution syntax should be included.
   - The function checks for prefixes after trimming trailing whitespace, which correctly handles cases like `echo test | sudo cat`.
   - Patterns with trailing spaces (e.g., "sudo ") may not match if there are multiple spaces or tabs before the command. Consider normalizing whitespace or using regex for pattern matching.

3. **Performance**:
   - The `matchesAtCommandPosition` function uses `strings.Index` in a loop, which is O(n*m) in the worst case. For typical command lengths, this is negligible, but consider benchmarking if commands can be very long.

4. **Pattern Maintenance**:
   - The `commandPatterns` map requires manual updates when new deny patterns are added. Consider adding a comment or validation to remind developers to categorize new patterns appropriately.
   - Patterns with trailing spaces may be error-prone. Consider a helper function to normalize pattern definitions.

   - `Sample()` applies history penalties before sampling

3. **Penalty Logic** (`sample/transforms.go`):
   - New `applyPenalty()` function implementing:
     - Repeat penalty: divides positive logits, multiplies negative logits by `repeatPenalty`
     - Frequency penalty: subtracts `count * frequencyPenalty` from logit
     - Presence penalty: subtracts `presencePenalty` once per token

4. **Runner Integration** (`runner/ollamarunner/runner.go`):

   ```go

       history = make([]int32, 0, DefaultPenaltyLookback)
       counts = make(map[int32]int, DefaultPenaltyLookback)
   }
   ```
   This avoids unnecessary memory allocation and computation for users who do not use these features.

3. **Correct Repeat Penalty Behavior**: The implementation preserves the ordering of negative logits when applying repeat penalty:
   ```go
   if logit < 0 {
       logit *= repeatPenalty  // More negative = less likely
   } else {
       logit /= repeatPenalty  // Less positive = less likely
   }
   ```
   This is mathematically correct and prevents unintended behavior.

4. **Sliding Window History**: The `Accept()` method maintains a fixed-size history window (`DefaultPenaltyLookback = 64`), automatically evicting old tokens. This bounds memory usage and focuses penalties on recent context.

# Code Review: runner/ollamarunner - Graceful Error Handling for Sampling/Decoding Failures

## Overview
This change addresses issue #14718 by replacing panic calls with graceful error handling in the ollamarunner. When token sampling or decoding fails for a single sequence, the runner now terminates only that sequence instead of crashing the entire process, allowing other concurrent sequences to continue being served.

---

## Analysis

### Changes Summary

1. **New DoneReason Constant** (`llm/server.go`):
   ```go
   // DoneReasonError indicates the completion stopped due to an internal error
   DoneReasonError
   ```
   Added to the `DoneReason` type with corresponding `String()` method returning "error".

2. **Error Handling in Sampling** (`runner/ollamarunner/runner.go`):
   ```go
   // Before:
   if err != nil {
       panic("failed to sample token")
   }
   
   // After:
   if err != nil {
       slog.Error("failed to sample token", "seq": seq.cache.Id, "error", err)
       s.removeSequence(i, llm.DoneReasonError)
       continue
   }
   ```

3. **Error Handling in Decoding**: Same pattern applied to token decoding failures.

---

## Strengths

1. **Improved Fault Isolation**: Errors affecting a single sequence no longer terminate the entire runner process. This is critical for multi-tenant or batch serving scenarios where one malformed request should not impact others.

2. **Consistent Error Handling Pattern**: The fix follows the existing pattern used throughout the function for EOS, length limits, and connection closures:
   ```go
   s.removeSequence(i, llm.DoneReasonStop)  // or other reason
   continue
   ```
   This consistency improves code maintainability and reduces cognitive load.

3. **Structured Logging**: Using `slog.Error` with contextual fields (`seq`, `error`, `token`) enables better observability and debugging compared to panic messages.

4. **Clean Resource Cleanup**: Calling `removeSequence` ensures proper cleanup of sequence state, preventing resource leaks that could occur with abrupt panic termination.

5. **Minimal and Focused**: The change is surgical, addressing only the specific panic calls without refactoring surrounding logic, reducing regression risk.

6. **New DoneReason Value**: Adding `DoneReasonError` allows downstream consumers to distinguish error-induced terminations from normal completion reasons, enabling appropriate client-side handling.

---

## Considerations

1. **Error Propagation to Clients**: Verify that the `DoneReasonError` value is properly communicated to API clients. If clients expect specific error formats or status codes, ensure the runner translates this reason appropriately in the HTTP response.

2. **Logging Level**: Using `slog.Error` is appropriate for unexpected failures. However, consider whether some sampling/decoding errors might be expected (e.g., malformed input) and should be logged at `Warn` level instead. This depends on the error types returned by `Sample()` and `Decode()`.

3. **Sequence ID Availability**: The log includes `seq.cache.Id`. Verify that this ID is always populated and meaningful for debugging. If sequences can be created without IDs, consider fallback logging.

4. **Error Type Discrimination**: The current handling treats all errors from `Sample()` and `Decode()` identically. If certain errors are recoverable (e.g., temporary resource exhaustion) while others are fatal (e.g., model corruption), consider differentiating the handling:
   ```go
   var recoverable RecoverableError
   if errors.As(err, &recoverable) {
       // Retry logic or different cleanup
   } else {
       s.removeSequence(i, llm.DoneReasonError)
   }
   ```

5. **DoneReason String Representation**: The `String()` method returns "error" for `DoneReasonError`. This is clear but generic. Consider whether a more specific string (e.g., "internal_error") would aid log parsing or client handling.

---

## Potential Issues

1. **Silent Failure Risk**: After logging and removing the sequence, the error is not propagated further. If upstream components need to know about the failure (e.g., for metrics or alerting), ensure additional instrumentation exists.

2. **Resource Cleanup Completeness**: Verify that `removeSequence` properly releases all resources associated with the sequence, including:
   - Sampler state
   - Token buffers
   - Cache entries
   - Any goroutines or channels specific to the sequence

3. **Concurrent Modification**: The `continue` statement skips to the next sequence in the batch. Ensure that removing a sequence does not invalidate indices or iterators used elsewhere in the loop.

4. **Testing Coverage**: The change should be covered by tests that:
   - Simulate sampling/decoding errors
   - Verify the failing sequence is terminated
   - Verify other sequences continue processing
   - Verify proper logging occurs

   - Whether restarts are needed or if errors are self-contained

## Overview
This change fixes a bug in the Anthropic-compatible API layer where the `thinking.type="disabled"` parameter was not being properly converted to the native Ollama API format. The fix ensures that when users explicitly disable thinking via the Anthropic API, the `think` parameter is correctly set to `false` in the converted request.

---

## Analysis

### The Bug
**Before:**
```go
if r.Thinking != nil && r.Thinking.Type == "enabled" {
    think = &api.ThinkValue{Value: true}
}
```

**After:**
```go
if r.Thinking != nil {
    if r.Thinking.Type == "enabled" {
        think = &api.ThinkValue{Value: true}
    } else if r.Thinking.Type == "disabled" {
        think = &api.ThinkValue{Value: false}
    }
}
```

### Why This Matters
- The original code only set the `think` parameter when `thinking.type` was `"enabled"`.
- When `thinking.type` was `"disabled"`, the `think` parameter was omitted entirely from the converted request.
- The native Ollama API treats a missing `think` parameter as "use model default", which for qwen3.5 means thinking is enabled.
- This caused inconsistent behavior: users explicitly disabling thinking still received thinking content.

---

           think = &api.ThinkValue{Value: true}

## Overview
This change introduces validation to detect and reject embedding vectors containing NaN or Infinity values before they are JSON-encoded. The validation is applied across multiple layers: the core `llm` package, both runner implementations (`llamarunner` and `ollamarunner`), and the HTTP route handler. A comprehensive test suite is also added.

Note: The PR title mentions "Add qwen3.5 to the TUI for recommendation" but the actual changes are unrelated to model recommendations. Verify that the title accurately reflects the change or consider splitting this into separate PRs.

---

## Analysis

### The Change Summary

1. **New Validation Function** (`llm/server.go`):
   ```go
   func ValidateEmbedding(embedding []float32) error {
       for _, v := range embedding {
           if math.IsNaN(float64(v)) || math.IsInf(float64(v), 0) {
               return errors.New("model produced invalid embedding values (NaN or Inf)")
           }
       }
       return nil
   }
   ```

2. **Test Coverage** (`llm/embedding_test.go`): 10 test cases covering valid embeddings, edge cases (empty, nil, zeros, negatives), and invalid values (NaN, Inf).

3. **Integration Points**:
   - `runner/llamarunner/runner.go`: Validation before JSON encoding
   - `runner/ollamarunner/runner.go`: Validation plus bug fix for double channel read
   - `server/routes.go`: Inline validation in HTTP handler

4. **Bug Fix**: In `ollamarunner/runner.go`, the embedding channel is now read once into a variable and reused, preventing a potential deadlock or data loss from reading the same channel twice.

---

## Strengths

1. **Prevents JSON Encoding Errors**: Go's `json.Marshal` fails with "unsupported value" when encountering NaN or Inf. This validation provides a clear, actionable error message instead of a cryptic marshaling failure.

2. **Comprehensive Test Coverage**: The test suite covers:
   - Valid cases: normal values, empty slice, nil, zeros, negative numbers
   - Invalid cases: NaN at various positions, positive/negative Inf, all-NaN vectors
   - Table-driven tests with descriptive names for easy maintenance

3. **Defensive Programming**: Validating at multiple layers (runner and server) ensures that invalid embeddings are caught even if one validation layer is bypassed.

4. **Bug Fix Included**: The fix in `ollamarunner/runner.go` addresses a subtle concurrency issue where `<-seq.embedding` was being read twice, which could cause a goroutine leak or panic.

5. **Clear Error Messages**: The error message explicitly states what went wrong and where, aiding debugging for model developers.

1. **Redundant Validation**: The same check appears in three places:
   - `llm.ValidateEmbedding()` (called by runners)
   - Inline check in `server/routes.go`

   // Alternative using float32-native checks
   if v != v { // NaN check for float32
       return errors.New("embedding contains NaN")
   }
   if v == math.MaxFloat32 || v == -math.MaxFloat32 { // Approximate Inf check
       // More robust: use bits to check exponent

I've dug through the history of the `llamafile` portion of `ggml-cpu` to make sure this is the right place for these additional CGO flags to live, and my conclusion is that it is!

For background, the `llamafile` portion of `ggml` was added in https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/6414. This was an effort from the maintainer of [llamafile](https://github.com/mozilla-ai/llamafile) to upstream improvements made in that project. In the PR, these improvements are framed as general-purpose improvements to MM on CPU and are _not_ specific to the usage of `llama.cpp` in the `llamafile` project (as I had originally thought). [The comment from Georgi](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/6414#pullrequestreview-1991324849) discussed the coupling of this code to the core of `ggml`. When it was first merged, it looks like there was some hesitance on the coupling, but it seems that since then this has become the standard path for CPU optimizations.

Given all that, I believe adding these `go` modules alongside the `llamafile` portion of `ggml` is the right way to go to enable these platform-specific flags!

This PR brings in a collection of new architecture-specific implementation files for `ggml-cpu`. Those should be relatively trivial to include, though the maintainers will need to agree that they want to support `powerpc` as a CPU backend target. Assuming they want to add this support, you'll need to update `ml/backend/ggml/ggml/.rsync-filter` to include them.

Additionally, there are a number of changes in this PR that make changes to the sync'ed files in `ml/backend/ggml/ggml/src`. These changes can't be made directly since those source files are automatically copied from `llama.cpp` during the dependency bump process. Instead, you'll need to go through the dependency bump process and create a new patch with these changes (more details below). There also appear to be couple of changes in `simd-mappings.h` and `arch-fallback.h` that may effect other backends, so these will need to be validated as non-breaking on other platforms.

## Sync process

The process loosely looks like:

1. Check out the right hash of `llama.cpp` in `llama/vendor` (`make -f Makefile.sync llama/vendor clean checkout`)
2. Apply the current patches to the working copy in `llama/vendor` (`make -f Makefile.sync apply-patches`)
3. Make edits directly in `llama/vendor` for the changes you need on top of `llama.cpp`'s code
4. Commit them in `llama/vendor`
5. Make the new patch (`make -f Makefile.sync format-patches`)
6. Sync from `llama/vendor` over to the version that will be committed in `llama/llama.cpp` and `ml/backend/ggml` (`make -f Makefile.sync sync`)
7. Make sure everything builds and works
8. Commit the new patch file and the updates to the vendor'ed code in `llama/llama.cpp` and `ml/backend/ggml`
